> **Marcus** · cohort peer

Reading this, the fix seems obvious though? If `k=8` is the binding constraint, set `k=20`. You said yourself that widening N does not create a ninth slot — so create twelve more slots.

What am I missing that makes this not the first thing to try?

replies.body:
> **Dana** · reviewer · owns the eval harness

You are not missing anything about the mechanism — raising `k` genuinely does move full-chain recall. What you are missing is the second column.

Measured on the same 207 questions, structural chunking, same reranker:

```
 k   full_chain_recall   context_precision   prompt tokens   $/1k queries
 4         0.361              0.71               2,180          $ 6.55
 8         0.469              0.52               4,090          $12.27
16         0.548              0.31               7,910          $23.73
32         0.591              0.17              15,400          $46.20
```

Full-chain recall is still climbing at `k=32`. So is the bill, faster. And `context_precision` — the share of packed chunks that are actually gold — has fallen through the floor: at `k=32` roughly **five of every six chunks the model reads are irrelevant**.

That matters beyond cost, because `answer_correct` does *not* track full-chain recall up this curve. It peaks around `k=12–16` on this corpus and then declines, which is the "lost in the middle" effect [#38](https://github.com/akash-coded/nanorag/discussions/38) is about. **You can retrieve the evidence and still lose the answer by burying it.**

So raising `k` is the correct first experiment and the wrong place to stop. It is the blunt instrument the answer above lists first for exactly that reason.

> **Marcus** · cohort peer

That is a much better table than the one in my head. The `context_precision` column is the one I would never have looked at — I was treating "did the gold arrive" as the only question.

So the packing constraint from notebook 02 buys the same recall at `k=8` that raising `k` buys at ~16, without the precision collapse. That is the actual argument.

comments.body:
> **Rafael** · cohort peer · came from search infra

A question about the arithmetic rather than the fix, because I want to check I understand what full-chain recall *is*.

If per-passage recall is 0.938 at `N=100`, and a two-hop question needs both passages, should full-chain not be about `0.938² = 0.880`? The measured number is `0.469`. That is not a small discrepancy, it is off by a factor of nearly two.

Either I have the wrong model of the metric or something else is going on.

replies.body:
Your model is right; it is being applied at the wrong stage. This is worth spelling out because it is the single most common thing people get wrong about multi-hop retrieval, and it comes up in interviews constantly.

**`0.938` is Recall@N — the candidate pool of 100.** **`0.469` is full-chain recall over the packed context of `k=8`.** Different denominators, different stages. Compare like with like and the picture is different:

```
full_chain_recall_at_N   (over the N=100 pool)   0.871
full_chain_recall        (over the k=8 packed)   0.469
```

`0.871` against your predicted `0.880` — the conjunction model is essentially right at that stage. **The entire gap from 0.871 to 0.469 happens during packing.** That is the number that says where the work is.

**Now the more interesting half of your question: why is `0.871` slightly *above* `0.938² = 0.880`?** It is not — it is slightly below, but only just, and both are much higher than independence would give across the whole set, because independence is the wrong assumption.

Two gold passages for one question are frequently in the **same document**, or in documents that share entities and therefore co-retrieve. Retrieving one makes retrieving the other more likely, not independent of it. Formally, `P(A∧B) = P(A)·P(B|A)` and `P(B|A) > P(B)` here. Positive correlation lifts the conjunction above the independence floor.

So the independence estimate is a **lower bound worth computing**, because:

- if measured ≈ predicted, your hops are genuinely independent — usually means evidence is scattered and packing has to work hard;
- if measured ≫ predicted, your hops co-occur — often means your chunking has split one coherent passage in two, which is worth knowing;
- if measured ≪ predicted, something is actively suppressing the second hop. **Dedup by document is the usual culprit** — a diversity constraint that caps chunks per document will systematically drop the second hop of a same-document pair.

That last one has bitten this repo. It is why `pack_context` takes the constraint as a parameter rather than hard-coding it.

> **Rafael** · cohort peer · came from search infra

`full_chain_recall_at_N` being a separate field is the bit I had not registered — I was comparing the wrong two numbers.

The dedup-by-document failure mode is a good one. On my previous job we had exactly that and diagnosed it for a fortnight as an embedding problem.

> **the original poster** · cohort

Closing the loop. Ran the diagnostic from the accepted answer:

```
found-then-dropped: 84 of 207 questions
  comparison   41
  temporal     22
  inference    17
  null          4
```

84 questions where the evidence was in the pool and did not survive packing — against 27 where it was never retrieved at all. **My bottleneck was three-to-one on the stage I was not working on.**

Implemented the per-entity slot reservation from notebook 02 §2.2 for `comparison` questions only:

```
full_chain_recall   0.469 → 0.531   CI [+0.021, +0.104]   real
context_precision   0.52  → 0.51    (unchanged)
prompt tokens       4,090 → 4,140   (+1.2%)
```

Same `k`, same candidates, +0.062 for 1.2% more tokens. Raising `k` to 16 bought +0.079 for **93% more tokens** and wrecked precision. Not close.
